claim: Electrophysiological recordings allow for monitoring the operation of proteins with high temporal resolution down to the single molecule level.
source: Electrophysiological recordings allow for monitoring the operation of proteins with high temporal resolution down to the single molecule level.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the capabilities of electrophysiological recording techniques.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings have been exploited to track either ion flow arising from channel opening or the synchronized movement of charged residues and/or ions within the membrane electric field.
source: This technique has been exploited to track either ion flow arising from channel opening or the synchronized movement of charged residues and/or ions within the membrane electric field.
evidence: This is established knowledge about applications of electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Transient currents are elicited on rapid application of specific SERT inhibitors.
source: We examined transient currents elicited on rapid application of specific SERT inhibitors.
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental observations of transient currents upon SERT inhibitor application.

claim: The currents elicited by SERT inhibitors originate from ligand binding and not from a long-range conformational change.
source: Our analysis shows that these currents originate from ligand binding and not from a long-range conformational change.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Gouy-Chapman model predicts that adsorption of charged ligands to surface proteins must produce displacement currents and related apparent changes in membrane capacitance.
source: The Gouy-Chapman model predicts that adsorption of charged ligands to surface proteins must produce displacement currents and related apparent changes in membrane capacitance.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the Gouy-Chapman model.

claim: The predictions of the Gouy-Chapman model regarding displacement currents and capacitance changes were verified with SERT.
source: Here we verified these predictions with SERT.
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental verification of theoretical predictions.

claim: Ligand binding to a protein can be monitored in real time and in a label-free manner by recording the membrane capacitance.
source: Our observations demonstrate that ligand binding to a protein can be monitored in real time and in a label-free manner by recording the membrane capacitance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Voltage-clamp recordings have been used for the past 70 years to assess currents through membranes.
source: Voltage-clamp recordings have been used for the past 70 years to assess currents through membranes, which are either resistive (i.e. ion flux through ion channels, Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952) or which arise from synchronized movement of charged residues or ions within the membrane electric field (i.e. gating currents, Armstrong and Bezanilla, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical work by Hodgkin and Huxley (1952) and Armstrong and Bezanilla (1973).

claim: It is technically feasible to monitor currents through single molecules and to resolve conformational transitions which occur on the microsecond scale.
source: it is technically feasible to monitor currents through single molecules and to resolve conformational transitions, which occur on the microsecond scale.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the capabilities of electrophysiological techniques.

claim: Voltage-clamp recordings allow for determining the cell membrane capacitance (CM).
source: In addition, voltage-clamp recordings also allow for determining the cell membrane capacitance (CM).
evidence: This is established knowledge about voltage-clamp recording capabilities.

claim: It has been possible to detect changes in membrane area that result from the fusion of a single vesicle with the plasma membrane using capacitance measurements.
source: Using this approach, it has been possible to detect changes in membrane area that result from the fusion of a single vesicle with the plasma membrane (Neher and Marty, 1982; Fernandez et al., 1984; von Gersdorff and Matthews, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to work by Neher and Marty (1982), Fernandez et al. (1984), and von Gersdorff and Matthews (1994).

claim: A change in membrane area is not the only factor that can affect capacitance.
source: However, a change in membrane area is not the only factor that can affect capacitance.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about factors affecting membrane capacitance.

claim: Mobile charges within membrane proteins contribute to the total membrane capacitance in cells that overexpress a membrane protein.
source: Several studies – most of them conducted in cells that overexpressed a membrane protein – demonstrated the contribution of the same to the CM: the effect can be accounted for by mobile charges within the protein.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple studies.

claim: The total membrane capacitance of a cell expressing voltage-gated channels comprises a voltage-independent component ascribed to the membrane and a voltage-dependent component attributed to mobile charges within the voltage sensors of the channel.
source: Voltage-gated channels were the first membrane proteins on which capacitance measurements were conducted: the total CM of a cell expressing these proteins was shown to comprise a voltage-independent component, which was ascribed to the membrane, and a voltage-dependent component, which was attributed to mobile charges within the voltage sensors of the channel (Bean and Rios, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bean and Rios (1989).

claim: It has been possible to infer the conformational transition associated with phosphorylation of the Na+/K+-pump from the recorded change in capacitance.
source: it has, for instance, been possible to infer the conformational transition associated with phosphorylation of the Na+/K+-pump from the recorded change in capacitance (Lu et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lu et al. (1995).

claim: Binding of the co-substrate Cl- to the inward-facing conformation of GAT1 caused a very rapid reduction in the recorded capacitance.
source: Similarly, binding of the co-substrate Cl- to the inward-facing conformation of the γ-aminobutyric acid transporter-1 (GAT1/SLC6A1) caused a very rapid reduction in the recorded capacitance, which was proposed to reflect the suppression of a charge moving reaction induced by binding of Na+ to the outward -facing conformation of GAT1.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental observations on GAT1.

claim: Current and capacitance measurements were conducted in HEK293 cells expressing human SERT.
source: In the present study, we conducted current and capacitance measurements in HEK293 cells expressing human SERT.
evidence: This describes the experimental system used in the study.

claim: SERT is a member of the solute carrier 6 (SCL6) family.
source: Like GAT1, SERT is a member of the solute carrier 6 (SCL6) family.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SERT classification.

claim: The transport cycle of SERT is understood in considerable detail.
source: The transport cycle of SERT is understood in considerable detail (Schicker et al., 2012; Sandtner et al., 2014), in particular the nature of substrate-induced currents, electrogenic steps associated with binding and release of co-substrate ions and decision points in the transport cycle (Hasenhuetl et al., 2016; Kern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: SERT has a very rich pharmacology.
source: In addition SERT, in contrast to GAT1, has a very rich pharmacology (Sitte and Freissmuth, 2015), which allows for probing the actions of inhibitors (Hasenhuetl et al., 2015), atypical inhibitors (Sandtner et al., 2016), substrates and releasers (Sandtner et al., 2014; Kern et al., 2017), and atypical substrates/partial releasers (Bhat et al., 2017) by electrophysiological recordings.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A reduction in membrane capacitance was seen regardless of whether the ligand was the cognate substrate or an inhibitor of SERT.
source: A reduction in CM was seen regardless of whether the ligand was the cognate substrate or an inhibitor of SERT, e.g. cocaine.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental observations.

claim: Rapid application of 5-HT to SERT gives rise to an initial peak current followed by a steady-state current when measured in the whole cell configuration.
source: When measured in the whole cell configuration, rapid application of 5-HT to SERT gives rise to an initial peak current, which is followed by a steady-state current (Schicker et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schicker et al. (2012).

claim: The peak current elicited by 5-HT is caused by a synchronized conformational rearrangement that carries 5-HT through the membrane.
source: The peak current is caused by a synchronized conformational rearrangement that carries 5-HT through the membrane (Hasenhuetl et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hasenhuetl et al. (2016).

claim: The steady-state current elicited by 5-HT is contingent on the progression of SERT through the transport cycle.
source: The steady-state current on the other hand is contingent on the progression of SERT through the transport cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on understanding of SERT function.

claim: Raising intracellular Na+ impedes the SERT transport cycle and eliminates the steady-state current.
source: Raising intracellular Na+ impedes this cycle and eliminates the steady-state current (Hasenhuetl et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hasenhuetl et al. (2015).

claim: Application of 100 µM cocaine to a cell expressing SERT produces a cocaine-induced current that is smaller than that elicited by 30 µM 5-HT.
source: The recording in the lower panel of Figure 1A shows a cocaine-induced current, which was smaller than that elicited by 5-HT and which was absent in control cells (data not shown): In paired measurement, where cells were challenged with both 30 µM 5-HT and 100 µM cocaine (Figure 1B), we observed a constant amplitude ratio (5-HT: cocaine ~4:1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: The cocaine-induced current was absent in control cells.
source: The recording in the lower panel of Figure 1A shows a cocaine-induced current, which was smaller than that elicited by 5-HT and which was absent in control cells (data not shown)
evidence: This is stated as an observation from control experiments.

claim: The KD for cocaine binding to SERT has been estimated to range from 100 nM to 3 µM.
source: The KD for cocaine binding to SERT has been estimated by radioligand binding assays, by the concentration dependence of its inhibitory action on substrate uptake and by electrophysiological means (Hasenhuetl et al., 2015). The affinity estimates provided by these measurements range from 100 nM to 3 µM (Han and Gu, 2006; Hasenhuetl et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Han and Gu (2006) and Hasenhuetl et al. (2015).

claim: An increase in cocaine concentration was associated with larger amplitudes and accelerated peak current decays.
source: It is evident from these recordings that an increase in cocaine concentration was associated with larger amplitudes and accelerated peak current decays.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The time courses of the cocaine-induced current decays were adequately fit by a monoexponential function.
source: The time courses of the decays were adequately fit by a monoexponential function.
evidence: This describes the analysis method used for the data.

claim: The rates of cocaine-induced current decay increased linearly over the tested concentration range.
source: In Figure 1D, we plotted the rate estimates by the fits as a function of the applied cocaine concentration. The rates increased linearly over the tested concentration range.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At concentrations below 10 µM, cocaine failed to evoke detectable currents.
source: At concentrations below 10 µM, cocaine failed to evoke detectable currents.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Binding of competitive inhibitors to SERT is dependent on Na+.
source: Binding of competitive inhibitors to SERT is dependent on Na+ (Korkhov et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Korkhov et al. (2006).

claim: 100 µM cocaine failed to elicit a current in the absence of extracellular Na+.
source: Therefore, we measured the cocaine peak in the absence of extracellular Na+: at this condition, 100 µM cocaine failed to elicit a current (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: When Cl- was removed from the extracellular solution, the cocaine-induced currents were present but featured smaller amplitudes.
source: In contrast, when Cl- was removed from the extracellular solution, the cocaine-induced currents were present, but featured smaller amplitudes (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F and 1G.

claim: The cocaine peak became larger at positive potentials.
source: It is evident from Figure 2A that the cocaine peak became larger at positive potentials.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The current-voltage relation for the cocaine-induced peak current was linear over the explored voltage range and had a negative slope.
source: The current-voltage relation was examined by averaging nine independent experiments after normalizing the current amplitudes to the current recorded at +30 mV: this current-voltage relation was linear over the explored voltage range and had a negative slope (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Extracellular Cl- is required for SERT-mediated substrate uptake.
source: It has long been known that extracellular Cl- is required for SERT-mediated substrate uptake (Lingjaerde, 1971; Nelson and Rudnick, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lingjaerde (1971) and Nelson and Rudnick (1982).

claim: The presence of Cl- is not required for 5-HT binding to SERT.
source: However, the presence of Cl- is not required for 5-HT binding to SERT (Nelson and Rudnick, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nelson and Rudnick (1982).

claim: The absence of Cl- precludes the conversion of the substrate-loaded outward-facing transporter to the inward-facing conformation.
source: In fact, the absence of Cl- precludes the conversion of the substrate-loaded outward-facing transporter to the inward-facing conformation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SERT function.

claim: Removal of Cl- reduced the peak amplitude and the area under the peak of the 5-HT-induced current.
source: Removal of Cl- reduced the peak amplitude and the area under the peak (see Figure 3A for representative current traces and Figure 3B for the comparison of 20 independent experiments with paired recordings done in the presence and absence of Cl-).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: In the presence of Cl-, the current-voltage relation for the 5-HT-induced peak current had a positive slope.
source: in contrast to the positive slope seen in the presence of Cl- (Figure 3C,D), the slope was negative in the absence of Cl- (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: In the absence of Cl-, the current-voltage relation for the 5-HT-induced peak current had a negative slope.
source: in contrast to the positive slope seen in the presence of Cl- (Figure 3C,D), the slope was negative in the absence of Cl- (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: The absence of Cl- unmasked an event preceding the substrate-induced conformational change that had a small current amplitude and a negative slope in the current-voltage relationship.
source: These observations indicated that the absence of Cl- unmasked an event preceding the substrate-induced conformational change: this initial event had a small current amplitude and a negative slope in the current-voltage relationship.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The negative slope in the current-voltage relation was inconsistent with the conjecture that the cocaine-induced peak current originated from charges moving in the membrane electric field.
source: However, it is difficult to reconcile this with the negative slope in the current-voltage relation of both the cocaine- and the 5-HT-induced peak current in the absence of Cl-. The negative slope in the current-voltage relation was inconsistent with the conjecture that the cocaine-induced peak current originated from charges moving in the membrane electric field.
evidence: This is an inference based on the principles of electrostatics.

claim: The rules of electrostatics dictate that inwardly directed currents must increase at negative voltages if they are carried by charges moving in response to a conformational change.
source: The rules of electrostatics dictate that inwardly directed currents must increase at negative voltages, if they are carried by charges moving in response to a conformational change.
evidence: This is a statement of fundamental principles of electrostatics.

claim: The number of SERT molecules in the stable cell line was estimated to be 2 ± 0.4 × 10^7 transporters/cell.
source: in our stable cell line SERT is expressed at high levels; the number of SERT molecules was estimated in saturation binding experiments of [3H]imipramine and amounted to 2 ± 0.4 × 107 transporters/cell.
evidence: This is based on saturation binding experiments.

claim: If all SERT moieties are saturated by stoichiometric binding of one positively charged ligand per SERT, the charge density at the outer surface is expected to change by about ∆+0.0011 C/m^2.
source: If all SERT moieties are saturated by stoichiometric binding (one positively charged ligand/SERT), the charge density at the outer surface is expected to change by about ∆+0.0011 C/m2.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the number of SERT molecules and stoichiometric binding.

claim: The total surface charge density on the outer surface of untransfected HEK293 cells is about −0.005 C/m^2.
source: The total surface charge density on the outer surface of untransfected HEK293 cells is about −0.005 C/m2 (Zhang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al. (2001).

claim: The ligand-induced change in outer surface charge density changes Фt by about – 10 mV.
source: The ligand-induced change in outer surface charge density changes Фt by about – 10 mV (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by calculations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The simulated displacement currents based on the Gouy-Chapman model are inwardly directed with amplitudes in the low picoampere range and match the observed currents.
source: Figure 4B depicts simulated displacement currents based on the voltage estimates provided by the model. The simulated currents are inwardly directed with amplitudes in the low picoampere range and thus match the observed currents.
evidence: This is supported by simulations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: At low cocaine concentrations, the simulated currents compared favorably with the observed currents.
source: At low cocaine concentrations, the simulated currents compared favorably with the observed.
evidence: This is a comparison between simulated and experimental data.

claim: At higher cocaine concentrations, the predictions deviated from the measured kapp due to the solution exchange rate becoming rate-limiting.
source: However, at higher cocaine concentrations the predictions deviated from the measured kapp (red solid line in Figure 4D). We attribute this discrepancy to the fact that, at concentrations exceeding 30 µM, the solution exchange by our application device (~20 s−1) becomes rate-limiting
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of simulated and experimental data.

claim: The hypothesis that charged ligand binding results in the generation of a displacement current provides a parsimonious explanation for the negative slope of the observed current-voltage relation.
source: The hypothesis that charged ligand binding results in the generation of a displacement current therefore provides a parsimonious explanation for the negative slope of the observed current-voltage relation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling and experimental data.

claim: Application of 100 µM cocaine reduced the membrane capacitance in HEK293 cells expressing SERT.
source: Figure 5B shows a representative recording of the membrane capacitance (CM) with the two other circuit parameters RM and RS upon application and subsequent removal of 100 µM cocaine to HEK293 cells expressing SERT.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was no cross talk between circuit parameters during cocaine application.
source: It is evident from this recording that there was no cross talk between circuit parameters.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The effect of cocaine on membrane capacitance was absent in control cells.
source: This effect of cocaine on CM was absent in control cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The reduction in membrane capacitance by 100 µM cocaine amounted to approximately 500 fF.
source: The reduction in CM by cocaine amounted to approx. 500 fF, which is in good agreement with the prediction (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The concentration-response curve for the cocaine-induced decrease in apparent membrane capacitance provided an EC50 estimate of 156 ± 41 nM.
source: These data were adequately fit by a saturation hyperbola, which provided an estimate for the affinity of cocaine to SERT (EC50 = 156 ± 41 nM; Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: The EC50 estimate for cocaine from capacitance measurements is in line with the published KD of cocaine.
source: This estimate is in line with the published KD of cocaine (Hasenhuetl et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with previously published data.

claim: In the presence of extracellular Cl-, the reduction in membrane capacitance induced by 100 µM 5-HT amounted to −340 ± 140 fF.
source: In the presence of extracellular Cl- the reduction in CM induced by 100 µM 5-HT amounted to −340 ± 140 fF (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The concentration-response curve for the 5-HT-induced apparent reduction in membrane capacitance provided an EC50 estimate of 1.4 ± 0.1 µM.
source: The resulting saturation hyperbola provided an estimate for the apparent affinity of 5-HT to SERT (EC50 = 1.4 ± 0.1 µM, Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Comparison of the apparent reduction of capacitance elicited by 100 µM cocaine and 100 µM 5-HT revealed no difference.
source: Comparison of the apparent reduction of capacitance elicited by 100 µM cocaine and 100 µM 5-HT revealed no difference as is seen by the similar magnitude of the reduction in paired recordings (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The 5-HT-induced reduction in capacitance in the absence of extracellular Cl- was similar to that observed in the presence of Cl-.
source: Figure 5K shows the reduction in apparent CM at a saturating concentration of 5-HT (100 µM) in the absence of extracellular Cl-. As can be seen the 5-HT-induced reduction in capacitance under this condition was similar to the one observed in the presence of Cl- (cf. Figure 5I and H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Application of cocaine reduced the membrane capacitance in SERT-expressing cells but not in control cells.
source: Consistent with the results shown in Figure 5A, application of cocaine reduced the CM in SERT-expressing cells (left panel in Figure 6A) but not in control cells (right panel in Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The simulated capacitance recordings using the Gouy-Chapman model recapitulated the experimental capacitance recordings.
source: We also simulated the recordings in SERT-expressing cells using the Gouy-Chapman model: these synthetic data recapitulated the capacitance recordings (cf. left panel in Figure 6A and Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by simulations shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The Gouy-Chapman model predicted the voltage-dependent change in capacitance observed in control cells.
source: It is important to note that the Gouy-Chapman model also predicted the voltage-dependent change in capacitance observed in control cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by simulations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cocaine-induced decrease in capacitance depends on the voltage in a linear manner.
source: It is evident that (i) the cocaine-induced decrease in capacitance depends on the voltage in a linear manner
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The experimental observations and the synthetic data for voltage-dependent capacitance changes are in reasonable agreement.
source: It is evident that (i) the cocaine-induced decrease in capacitance depends on the voltage in a linear manner, and (ii) that the experimental observations and the synthetic data are in reasonable agreement.
evidence: This is a comparison between experimental and simulated data.

claim: In the absence of cocaine, changes in voltage were followed by a slow change in capacitance in SERT-expressing cells, particularly when the prior voltage had been +50 mV.
source: However, there is one notable difference: in the absence of cocaine, changes in voltage were followed by a slow change in capacitance in SERT-expressing cells, in particular when the prior voltage had been +50 mV (inset Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The slow change in capacitance is specific to SERT-expressing cells because it is absent in control cells and inhibited by cocaine.
source: Nevertheless, this slow change in capacitance is specific to SERT-expressing cells, because it is absent in control cells and inhibited by cocaine.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of SERT-expressing and control cells.

claim: Application of 100 µM cocaine to cells expressing the dopamine transporter gave rise to currents with a current-voltage relation with a negative slope.
source: First, we challenged HEK293 cells expressing the dopamine transporter with cocaine: this gave rise to currents, which had a current-voltage relation with a negative slope (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rapid application of 100 µM desipramine produced an inwardly directed peak current.
source: Consistent with the results obtained with cocaine, we detected an inwardly directed peak current upon rapid application of 100 µM desipramine (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Application of 10 µM desipramine resulted in a drop in apparent membrane capacitance in cells expressing SERT but not in control cells.
source: We also recorded a drop in apparent CM when cells expressing SERT were challenged with 10 µM desipramine (representative trace in the left panel of Figure 7B). This was not seen in control cells (right panel of Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: At concentrations exceeding 10 µM, desipramine increased membrane capacitance in both SERT-expressing and control cells.
source: At concentrations exceeding 10 µM, desipramine increased CM in both SERT-expressing and control cells (representative traces in Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In SERT-expressing cells, the concentration-response curve for the desipramine-induced change in capacitance was biphasic with a decline in the low concentration range followed by an increase in the high concentration range.
source: Thus, in SERT-expressing cells, the concentration-response curve for the desipramine-induced change in capacitance was biphasic with a decline in the low concentration range followed by an increase in the high concentration range (full symbols in Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In untransfected control cells, only the ascending limb of the concentration-response curve for desipramine-induced capacitance change was seen.
source: In contrast, only the ascending limb of the concentration-response curve was seen in untransfected control cells (empty symbols in Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The increase in capacitance at high desipramine concentrations is the expected consequence of desipramine adsorption to the inner surface of the membrane.
source: We carried out a simulation based on this conjecture, which recapitulated the capacitance recordings (Figure 7E). Thus, the rise in capacitance was the expected consequence of desipramine adsorption to the inner surface of the membrane.
evidence: This is supported by simulations shown in Figure 7E.

claim: At pH 5.5, 30 µM desipramine caused a decrease in apparent membrane capacitance.
source: This was the case: at pH 5.5, 30 µM desipramine caused a decrease in apparent CM (left panel in Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: At pH 7.4, 30 µM desipramine elicited an increase in capacitance.
source: In contrast, at pH 7.4, 30 µM desipramine elicited an increase in capacitance (right panel in Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: When assessed in paired recordings at pH 7.4 and pH 5.5, 30 µM desipramine consistently produced a drop in capacitance at pH 5.5 but not at pH 7.4.
source: When assessed in paired recordings at pH 7.4 and pH 5.5, 30 µM desipramine consistently produced a drop in capacitance at pH 5.5 but not at pH 7.4 (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: In control cells, desipramine increased the capacitance at pH 7.4 but was ineffective at pH 5.5.
source: We also repeated these experiments in control cells (Figure 7H). As expected, desipramine increased the capacitance at pH 7.4 (∆CM ~300 fC) but was ineffective at pH 5.5.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Ibogaine stabilizes the inward-facing conformation of SERT and inhibits substrate uptake in a non-competitive fashion.
source: Ibogaine stabilizes the inward-facing conformation of SERT and inhibits substrate uptake in a non-competitive fashion (Jacobs et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jacobs et al. (2007).

claim: Application of 10 µM ibogaine resulted in a reduction of the membrane capacitance in SERT-expressing cells but not in control cells.
source: application of 10 µM ibogaine resulted in a reduction of the CM (upper panel in Figure 8A). This effect was absent in control cells (lower panel in Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The observations on ibogaine-induced capacitance changes unequivocally refute the idea that ibogaine binds to a cytosolic site on SERT.
source: Hence, these observations unequivocally refute the idea that ibogaine binds to a cytosolic site on SERT.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The data suggest that the ibogaine binding site is directly accessible from the extracellular face of the transporter.
source: Instead, our data suggest that the ibogaine binding site is directly accessible from the extracellular face of the transporter.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The difference in pH (7.4 vs 5.5) did not affect the response to ibogaine.
source: We also evaluated the ibogaine-induced change in CM in paired recordings at pH 5.5 and 7.4, which did not affect the response to ibogaine (Figure 8B)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The Gouy-Chapman model was developed more than a century ago to understand the distribution of diffusible ions residing on top of a charged and polarizable surface.
source: The Gouy-Chapman model was developed more than a century ago to understand the distribution of diffusible ions residing on top of a charged and polarizable surface (Gouy, 1909; Chapman, 1913).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gouy (1909) and Chapman (1913).

claim: The Gouy-Chapman model provides a conceptual framework to approach the electrical properties of a lipid bilayer.
source: While originally developed for a description of the interaction between dissolved ions and a metal electrode, this model also provides a conceptual framework to approach the electrical properties of a lipid bilayer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the applicability of the Gouy-Chapman model.

claim: Fixed charges in biological membranes arise primarily from the net negative charge of phospholipid head groups.
source: Fixed charges arise primarily from the net negative charge of phospholipid head groups (McLaughlin et al., 1971).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McLaughlin et al. (1971).

claim: Proteins which reside in or at the plasma membrane also contribute to the surface charges.
source: In addition, proteins which reside in or at the plasma membrane, also contribute to the surface charges (Green and Andersen, 1991; Madeja, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Green and Andersen (1991) and Madeja (2000).

claim: Surface charges are asymmetrically distributed with the inner membrane leaflet carrying a higher negative surface charge density.
source: In cells, these surface charges are asymmetrically distributed with the inner membrane leaflet carrying a higher negative surface charge density.
evidence: This is established knowledge about membrane charge distribution.

claim: Under voltage-clamp conditions, any binding reaction which results in adsorption of a charged ligand to the surface of the cell membrane must evoke a displacement current and an apparent change in capacitance.
source: Thus, the underlying theory predicts, under voltage-clamp conditions, any binding reaction which results in adsorption of a charged ligand to the surface of the cell membrane must evoke a displacement current and an apparent change in capacitance.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the Gouy-Chapman model.

claim: The current experiments are the first to demonstrate that binding reactions to surface proteins can be directly monitored by recording the predicted currents and the apparent changes of the membrane capacitance.
source: In spite of the veneration of the Gouy-Chapman model, the current experiments are – to the best of our knowledge - the first to demonstrate that binding reactions to surface proteins can be directly monitored by recording the predicted currents and the apparent changes of the membrane capacitance.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current work.

claim: Inhibitors such as cocaine and desipramine produced a displacement current and the related change in apparent membrane capacitance.
source: Inhibitors such as cocaine and desipramine produced a displacement current and the related change in apparent CM.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: Binding of cocaine and desipramine per se did not result in movement of mobile charges within the membrane electric field and was fully accounted for by the change in outer surface charge density caused by ligand adsorption.
source: Their binding per se did not result in movement of mobile charges within the membrane electric field and was fully accounted for by the change in outer surface charge density caused by ligand adsorption.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and analysis.

claim: The change in membrane capacitance is consistent with the average density of SERT in the cell line employed.
